case_name: Even v. El Al Israel Airlines Ltd.
text:
COURT FILE NO.:

00-CV-195822

DATE:
20060222

ONTARIO

SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE

B E T W E E N:

)

)

SHALOM EVEN

Plaintiff

))))))

Alan M. Kaufman
, for the Plaintiff

- and -

)

)

EL AL ISRAEL AIRLINES LIMITED, YOEL FELDSCHUH, MOSHE
SHAMAI, MICHAEL MAYER, RAMI FISCHER, STANLEY MORAIS

Defendants

)))

)))))

Julian Harris Porter
, for the Defendant, El Al
Israel Airlines Ltd.

HEARD:
June 1, 2 and 3, 2005  written submissions
completed by August 10, 2005

REASONS FOR JUDGMENT

KLOWAK, J.

[
1
]

The plaintiff Shalom Even ran a travel agency by
the name of Shalom K Tours Inc. which specialized in group travel from Canada
to Israel.

[
2
]

That business went bankrupt owing the defendant
El Al, one of its creditors, some $688,000.00.

[
3
]

It is the way that debt arose and the likelihood
of it happening again which forms the foundation of El Al's conduct and actions
of which the plaintiff complains in this proceeding.

[
4
]

El Al had granted Shalom K Travel Inc. as well
as other travel agencies the right to issue an El Al ticket and to do so at
discounted prices.  The right to issue tickets was granted by written agreement
and was a privilege bestowed by the airline upon the travel agency.  A part of
the written agreement with respect to this privilege provided that El Al could
terminate the agreement thereby withdrawing the privilege at any time.

[
5
]

The privilege would generally be referred to as
plating

an agency, and an agency would consider itself to be
plated
or have a
particular airlines
plates
.

[
6
]

All money collected by the agent for the sale of
such tickets, including any remuneration which the agent could claim, had to be
held in trust by the travel agent for the carrier until settlement.

[
7
]

BSP, an arm of the International Air Transport
Association, automatically withdrew funds from the trust fund on a weekly basis
to pay for tickets issued by the agency the previous week as well as to pay
agency commissions on those sales.

[
8
]

The plaintiff missed three consecutive BSP
payments while continuing to sell El Al tickets throughout and within three
days of the final BSP missed payment had incorporated another company called
Shalom K Tours 2000 Inc.

[
9
]

Although the plaintiff maintained throughout the
bankruptcy that Shalom K Tours Inc.  was itself owed a substantial amount of
the money which was to have been held in trust by way of commissions, he was
clearly in breach of the legal requirement to hold all of the ticket money in
trust.

[
10
]

He and his wife refused to disclose to El Al
where the trust money had gone.  In addition, El Al suspected that he and his
family were continuing to carry on the business through the new company.

[
11
]

El Al, regardless of the prior longstanding
business relationship with the plaintiff, was one of the creditors who
petitioned him into bankruptcy.

[
12
]

There is no issue that the plaintiff was the
directing mind of the company and was looked at in the industry as the person
running the business, even though the shares were owned by his son.  His
daughter and his wife were also in the travel business.

[
13
]

After the bankruptcy and because of it, the
plaintiff could no longer operate a travel agency but was limited to attaching
himself to some other agency.

[
14
]

It is interference by El Al in his attempts to
do so of which the plaintiff complains in this lawsuit.

[
15
]

Specifically, the plaintiff maintains that El Al
interfered with his contractual relations with two different agencies, namely
YYZ Travel and Payless Travel, without, however, causing a breach of the
contract between those agencies and the plaintiff.

[
16
]

The plaintiff also maintains there were nine
additional incidents where El Al unlawfully interfered with his business
relations or interests, but which do not involve a contractual relationship
between the plaintiff and anyone else.

[
17
]

I will first deal with all eleven events and whether
or not, taken individually or collectively, they constitute the tort of
unlawful interference with business relations.

[
18
]

I will then deal with the events related to YYZ
Travel and Payless Travel and whether or not those events constitute the tort
of interference with contractual relations.

[
19
]

In dealing with issues of credibility, I find
Mr. Even gave inconsistent testimony and his answers appeared to be tailored to
suit what was in his interest at the time.

[
20
]

For example, at one time he said commissions were
the biggest part of his employment with YYZ Travel but at another time that it
was his salary which was the most important to him.

[
21
]

He also appeared evasive in answering questions
concerning an article which appeared in the Catholic Register, going so far as
to at first refuse to read the article at trial and saying it was a waste of
the court's time.

[
22
]

He also appeared evasive when asked about the
concerns of El Al at the time of the bankruptcy in regards to the principles of
Shalom K Tours Limited continuing to make bookings and issuing tickets through
third party travel agents and being paid on a c.o.d. basis through Shalom K
Tours 2000 Inc., the newly incorporated company.

[
23
]

On the other hand, Mr. Even complains El Al did
not disclose or produce from its files any communications with the travel
agencies between 2000 through 2005, either from its head office in Israel or
its New York office.  Mr. Morais on behalf of El Al, testified this was a local
matter and that there simply was not anything in the head office file
concerning the plaintiff in that period of time.

[
24
]

Although in my view it would be reasonable to
assume there might have been something in El Al files, the evidence is simply
insufficient for me to find that there probably was and that the defence is
hiding it.

Interference with Business/Economic
Relations

[
25
]

After the company's bankruptcy, the plaintiff
went to work for Holiday Travel.  That agency also went bankrupt.

[
26
]

After that bankruptcy, a magazine by the name of
the Catholic Register interviewed an El Al representative, Mr. Morais, and
reported that El Al wanted "people to really check.  There's a lot of fly
by night organizations, and it's not fair to people.  It gives people a bad
taste to their experience of the Holy Land".

[
27
]

The balance of the article contained quotes from
the plaintiff Mr. Even.  I find those quotes were accurate since even Mr. Even
seemed to accept that they were, although he tended to be evasive and was
reluctant to answer questions in that regard.

[
28
]

The plaintiff's claim that the magazine article
was libelous was withdrawn prior to trial.

[
29
]

With respect to the tort of unlawful
interference in business relations, I find the article to be nothing more than
a reported interview which outlined accurate information and legitimate
concerns.  As such, it does not factually support the commission by El Al of
any tort.

[
30
]

The plaintiff also complained that when he and
his wife worked at YYZ Travel after the bankruptcy, YYZ would not let his wife
answer the telephone for fear El Al would be offended.  When Ms. Pelts from YYZ
Travel gave evidence herself however, she was not asked about this allegation
and I draw the reasonable inference that she would not have supported it.

[
31
]

Nor is there sufficient evidence to support the
plaintiff's complaint that El Al withheld airline tickets from one Reverend
Cantalon because of the plaintiff's involvement in arranging his travel.  Nor
do I find in all these circumstances that it is a reasonable inference.

[
32
]

The plaintiff has also not established on the balance
of probabilities that the ticketing problems of Yad Vashem were somehow related
to the issues El Al had with the plaintiff.

[
33
]

Consequently, the foregoing complaints do not
factually support the commission by El Al of any tort.

[
34
]

The remaining events are essentially factually
undisputed by the defence, which simply maintains El Al had the right to do
what it did.

[
35
]

Those remaining events include the following:

1.    Shortly after the bankruptcy, El Al advised the Israeli
Government Tourist Office, which was in the process of organizing a seminar to
promote travel to Israel, that it would not attend or participate if the
plaintiff or his daughter were to attend.

There is nothing which compelled El Al to attend any seminar
or trade show and as far as I can see nothing to prevent El Al from sharing
with the organizers of the show why it would not be attending.

I will, however, consider this conduct along with the
remaining events complained of when dealing with the law on unlawful
interference with business relations.

2.    El Al threatened Susie Klein, a travel agent with YYZ, that
tickets for a B'nai Brith travel group might be withheld if the plaintiff were
involved in issuing them.

3.    El Al intervened to prevent the plaintiff from establishing
himself as a Canadian agent for the American agency ITAS during the time the
plaintiff worked for YYZ Travel (Canadian Gateway Division).

4.    El Al advised two other agencies, being Travel For Less and
Amiel Tours, that retaining the services of the plaintiff would put El Al in a
precarious position.

5.    El Al informed YYZ Travel it was going to terminate its
written agreement which gave that agency the right to issue El Al tickets.  El
Al clearly told YYZ Travel it was doing so because YYZ employed the plaintiff.
The cancellation of the agreement between El Al and YYZ would have meant that
YYZ would no longer have the privilege of directly issuing El Al tickets or
enjoy the privilege of a discount price from El Al, that is, no longer have El
Al
plates
.

In any event, negotiations ensued and Ms. Pelts for YYZ
Travel made the business decision and it was agreed with El Al that the
plaintiff would remain with YYZ for the duration of his contract, his profile
with YYZ would be minimized, and his contract would not be renewed when it
expired.

Thus it is clear El Al interfered with the plaintiff's
employment with YYZ Travel even if in the end his contract with that agency was
not breached.

I will consider this event as part of the conduct related to
wrongful interference with business relations and as well will deal with it
when considering the tort of interference with contractual relations not
resulting in a breach of contract.

6.    The last situation, involving Payless Travel, is not very
clear.  Ms. Osovitski, a co-owner of Payless Travel testified that in the fall
of 2004 Payless Travel and the plaintiff were in a business relationship where
the plaintiff was organizing Christian and Jewish groups traveling to Tel
Aviv.

She said the plaintiff was only organizing hotels and tours in
Israel, not air flights which were on various airlines including El Al.

She says he had no office with them and no connection with the
computer but that he would make arrangements for a tour and send materials to
their offices.

In the fall of 2004, the Canadian Society for Yad Vashem approached
her for a quote and special itinerary for a group traveling from Canada to
Israel.

Plaintiff responded by letter dated November 21, 2004, signed by the
plaintiff as "vice president sales and marketing" for Payless.

The matter came to the attention of El Al and on December 6, 2004
Mr. Morais, the general manager contacted Ms. Osovitski and suggested it would
be better for Payless not to deal with the plaintiff because of the past
history.

Although she informed Mr. Morais that they would let the plaintiff
go, Ms. Osovitski also told him she had to keep the plaintiff on some other
projects because he had already developed a relationship with the people
involved.

The plaintiff confirmed in his testimony that his employment
position was to be vice president of sales and marketing with Payless at a
salary of $2,000 per month with 50% commission, credit card for expenses, and a
car.

He said he continues to do work for Payless but that he does not
know if he is going to be paid and takes his work day by day.

He said that since he started with Payless, he mainly books
passengers on Air Canada, has used Olympic Airlines a couple of times and has
nothing to do with El Al.

This seems to me inconsistent with Ms. Osovitski's testimony that he
only organizes hotels and tours and never air flights, thereby giving
considerable support to El Al's contention that no one can really monitor or
control him insofar as booking airlines is concerned.

El Al's concern is that where the agency for which Mr. Even works is

plated
by Al El, it enables Mr. Even to sell El Al tickets directly to a
customer and presumably thereby access monies which should be going into a
trust account.

In any event, Mr. Morais for El Al testified that if Payless wishes
to maintain the plaintiff as an employee, El Al would assess the situation and
if it felt it was a risk to the airline, El Al might revoke the Payless
plates
.

Thus, with respect to Payless, it is less clear that the
plaintiff has been prevented or hindered from performing his contract, in light
of the less than straightforward evidence in that regard.  I will nevertheless
deal with this complaint regarding Payless when considering both unlawful
interference with business relations and when considering interference with
contractual relations.

[
36
]

Until relatively recently the general position
of the common law has been that short of direct or indirect interference with
an existing contract, interference with economic relations did not constitute a
tort.  This position has been based on the rationale that maintaining and
facilitating free competition in the marketplace is of significant public
interest.
671122 Ontario Limited v. Sagaz Industries
(1998).

[
37
]

Common law now recognizes, however, an emerging
tort of wrongful interference with economic or business relations, liability
for which depends on proof of an unlawful act or acts directed against the
plaintiff's business relationship or business expectancy, with intent to cause
him or her harm.  G.H.L. Fridman, The Law of Torts in Canada, 2nd. ed.
(Toronto: Carswell, 2002) at 813-814.  Also see L. N. Klar, Tort Law, 3rd ed.
(Toronto: Thompson Carswell, 2003) at 637-640.

[
38
]

For example, in
Gershman v. Manitoba
Vegetable Producers’ Marketing Board
,

1976 CanLII 1093 (MB CA)
, [1976] 4 W.W.R. 406 (Man.
C.A.), which is discussed later in this judgment, O'Sullivan J.A. held that the
plaintiff lost not just the opportunity for formation of a contract but the
opportunity to further extend his already existing contractual relationship.

[
39
]

In
Dufferin Real Estate Ltd. v. Giralico
,

[1989] O.J. No. 1525 (QL)
Ewaschuk J. recognized the tort as one of unlawful
interference with legitimate business expectancy with the elements of the tort
being: (1) the existence of a valid business relationship or business
expectancy between the plaintiff and another party; (2) knowledge of this by
the defendant; (3) intentional interference which induces or causes a
termination of the business relationship or expectancy by unfair or unlawful
means; (4) proximate cause; and (6) resultant damages to the plaintiff.

[
40
]

One of the most recent cases to analyze the tort
of economic interference is the decision of the Ontario Court of Appeal in
Reach
M.D. Inc. v. Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada
(2003),
2003 CanLII 27828 (ON CA)
,
65 O.R. (3d) 30
(C.A.).  At issue in
Reach

was whether the Committee of the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of
Canada ("PMAC") interfered with the business relations of the
plaintiff manufacturer of medical calendars.  The Committee had issued a
"warning" to all of its members that endorsing the plaintiff's
calendar would lead to a potential contravention of the PMAC's Code of
Marketing Practices.  As a result of this "warning", the plaintiff
lost so much of its business that it had to cease manufacturing its calendar
altogether. The court considered whether the actions of the Committee were
directed at the plaintiff, whether they were lawful and whether they were the
cause of the plaintiff's damage.

[
41
]

The court identified the elements of the tort as
follows:

1.         intention to injure;

2.         interference
with the plaintiff's business by illegal or unlawful means; and

3.         consequential economic loss.

1.         intention to injure

[
42
]

In order to establish that the alleged
interference with economic relations was intentional, the Ontario Court of
Appeal found the plaintiff must show that the defendant's actions were
directed

or
targeted
at the plaintiff.  Evidence that the defendant was acting in
its own best interests and that the injury to the plaintiff was foreseeable,
were not sufficient to establish liability.

[
43
]

The Ontario Court of Appeal concluded, however,
that the plaintiff need not prove that the defendant's predominant purpose was
to injure the plaintiff.  Rather, this element is satisfied as long as the
unlawful act is in some measure directed against the plaintiff, even if
"its predominant interest was to advance its own interest and those of its
members"
Reach
at para. 46.  The court cited J. G. Fleming
Law
of Torts
, 9
th
ed. (Sydney: Law Book Company Ltd. 1998).

[
44
]

In the present case, I find El Al was extremely
concerned about Mr. Even working for a travel agency which El Al had
plated
,
not simply because it was owed some $688,000 due to the bankruptcy, but because
the plaintiff had breached his trust agreement with El Al and if he was in a
position to again issue El Al tickets through another travel agency, it might
happen again.

[
45
]

The plaintiff suggests that El Al made a point
of hunting the plaintiff down at the various agencies where he worked in order
to target him.

[
46
]

I find that was not the case, but rather El Al
found itself from time to time with information that the plaintiff was working
at one agency or another which was
plated
by El Al and might
consequently issue El Al tickets.

[
47
]

There was no way for El Al to supervise the work
done by the plaintiff to ensure that he had either no access to or did not
exercise access to computers at the travel agencies where he worked.  Anyone
accessing those computers could issue an El Al ticket.

[
48
]

However, although the predominant purpose of El
Al might well have been to protect itself and its trust monies from a repeat of
its past experience with the plaintiff, the various actions it took were
clearly directed at the plaintiff and El Al was fully cognizant of what
injurious effects its actions would have on the plaintiff.  It would be
difficult to find El Al did not intend the clearly foreseeable results, namely
that the various agencies might choose to retain El Al
plates
rather
than do business with the plaintiff.

2.         interference with the plaintiff's business by illegal or
unlawful means

[
49
]

Once the element of intention is satisfied, the
plaintiff must also establish that the defendant's interference with its
business was accomplished by illegal or unlawful means.

[
50
]

On this issue, the Ontario Court of Appeal in
Reach,
supra,
followed Lord Denning's dictum in
Torquay Hotel Co. Ltd. v.
Cousins
,
[1969] 1 All. E.R. 522 (C.A.)

and held unlawful means are
not just acts in violation of a statute or acts specifically prohibited by law,
but rather are acts which the defendant
is not at liberty to commit
.
[Emphasis added.]

[
51
]

The Committee in
Reach
was not at liberty
to commit the acts because it exceeded its authority in doing so.

[
52
]

The decision in
Reach
was followed by
Gates J. in
Drouillard v. Cogeco Cable Inc.,
[2005] O.J. No. 3166 (Sup.
Ct.) (QL)
.  In that case the plaintiff, who had been employed by Cogeco as a
cable and fibre network technician, had been blacklisted by Cogeco and was thus
unable to find other employment with contractors who worked for his former
employer.  Given Cogeco's virtual monopoly in the cable and fibre optic
business in the area, this left the plaintiff with no employment opportunities
within his area of specialization.  He alleged that this constituted
interference with his economic relations.

[
53
]

Gates J. found that Cogeco was liable for
unlawful interference with the plaintiff's business relations.  It is important
to point out that the prior employment evaluations of the plaintiff were
outstanding and he was highly regarded by his colleagues.  Thus, Cogeco had no
reason to "blacklist" him on the basis of prior poor performance.
What appeared to be the key concern of Cogeco was the plaintiff's prior attempt
to bring in a union.  The court held that Cogeco's actions were directed at the
plaintiff, were unlawful (they breached Cogeco's internal policy because Cogeco
had no reasonable cause to act in the way that it did) and caused damage to the
plaintiff.

[
54
]

In the present case, the defence argued that it
had every right to do what it did because its written agreements with the
various
plated
agencies could be terminated by El Al for any reason at
any time.  Secondly the defence argues that El Al had reasonable cause to
protect itself because of the prior interference by the plaintiff with its
trust monies.

[
55
]

The plaintiff on the other hand argued that the
actions complained of are part of a course of conduct by El Al, the result of
which is a restraint of the plaintiff's trade in that the plaintiff is
prohibited from carrying on his business as a travel consultant in tours from
Canada to Israel.

[
56
]

In my view the evidence did not clearly show that
the plaintiff was in the business of a travel consultant but rather he appeared
to work or be employed by other travel agencies, usually in sales or marketing.

[
57
]

On the evidence, the plaintiff held himself out
or described himself as a sales agent, as vice president of sales and
marketing, or as a general sales agent for Canada, depending on which company
he was with at the time.

[
58
]

Indeed it may very well be that he still works
for Payless Travel even though Payless Travel still has El Al
plates
.

[
59
]

Although he may not in fact have issued El Al
tickets since the bankruptcy, it is reasonable for El Al to be concerned that
he in fact could do so if working for a
plated
agency.

[
60
]

El Al has already had to shore up and maintain
its reputation by honouring tickets which he sold but for which El Al was never
paid as a result of the disappearance of trust funds and the bankruptcy.

[
61
]

In those circumstances, El Al was not acting out
of a sense of maliciousness or vindictiveness as was the case in
Gershman v.
Manitoba Vegetable Producers’ Marketing Board
, supra,
and in making sure it
did not find itself in the same business position with the plaintiff yet
another time, it did only what it was at liberty to do under the provisions of
its written agreements with the various agencies.

[
62
]

I also note that the agencies, as well as the
plaintiff, could still purchase El Al tickets, use another airline such as Air
Canada which also flies direct to Israel, or buy discount tickets including
flights on El Al from a consolidator.  Additionally, the plaintiff himself
could have worked for any other agency which was not
plated
by El Al.
The evidence was that there are about 5,000 travel agencies in Canada and only
about 400 of them can issue El Al tickets.

[
63
]

The plaintiff also argued that the defendant's
actions were unlawful since they were a restraint of trade.

[
64
]

The tort of wrongful interference with
business/economic relations is itself a tort in restraint of trade.  In
International
Brotherhood of Teamsters v. Therien
,
1960 CanLII 33 (SCC)
, [1960] S.C.R. 265 at 280, for
instance, Locke J. noted that a person is "not entitled to interfere with
another man’s method of gaining his living by illegal means."

[
65
]

Further, in
Nagle v. Feilden
,
[1966] 2
Q.B. 633 (C.A.) [
Nagle
]
which dealt with a Jockey Club that refused to
licence women jockeys, Lord Denning found that no contractual or membership
relationship was required to bring the action because "the true ground of
jurisdiction in all these cases is a man's right to work".
Nagel, supra

at 646.

[
66
]

It seems to me that the required element of
unlawfulness in a tort in restraint of trade cannot be restraint of trade
itself, or else the requirement of unlawfulness is rendered meaningless.

[
67
]

In the end, I find the acts of El Al were acts
it was at liberty to commit and thus the plaintiff' has not established the
acts of El Al were unlawful.

3.         consequential economic loss

[
68
]

It was argued on behalf of the plaintiff that
the actions of the defendant prohibited the plaintiff from carrying on his
business as a travel consultant in tours from Canada to Israel.

[
69
]

I have already found it was unclear whether the
plaintiff was a travel consultant and he appeared to more likely be simply an
employee.

[
70
]

Regardless, I am prepared to assume that the
last six complaints in their totality had a negative economic impact upon the
plaintiff even though there were few particulars of specific economic loss.

Interference with Contractual Relations

[
71
]

The plaintiff also submits that the two
incidents relating to YYZ Travel and Payless Travel involved an interference by
the defendant with the plaintiff's contract at YYZ and with his contract at
Payless Travel, and consequently, with respect to these two matters, the
plaintiff need not show that the defendant committed an illegal or unlawful
act.

[
72
]

El Al had informed YYZ Travel that it was going
to terminate its
plating
agreement with them if that agency continued to
employ the plaintiff.  After negotiation between El Al and YYZ, the plaintiff
remained with YYZ with a minimized profile for the duration of his contract,
which was not renewed when it expired.

[
73
]

At Payless, El Al in essence advised that agency
it would be better for them not to deal with the plaintiff.  It appears he
probably still does work for them although it is not clear what he does or what
he earns.

[
74
]

Traditionally, tort law imposed liability where
the defendant intentionally induced a party to a contract to break that
contract.

[
75
]

In
Torquay Hotel, supra,
the English
court expanded liability for inducing a breach of contract to those situations
where no breach occurred.  At issue in that case was whether the conduct of a
union preventing the delivery of heating oil to the plaintiff hotel amounted to
an interference with contractual relations between the hotel and the oil
suppliers, even though no actual breach of contract occurred.

[
76
]

In effect, this case established that an act of
interference which prevents or hinders fulfillment of a contract is actionable
even if there is no resultant breach.  It also established that whereas direct
interference was itself unlawful, indirect interference required an unlawful
act in order to be actionable.

[
77
]

In the present case, El Al took direct steps
with the plaintiff's employer YYZ Travel and subsequently with his employer
Payless Travel to hinder or prevent the continuing employment of the plaintiff
with those agencies if those agencies continued to enjoy the privilege of
having El Al
plates
.

[
78
]

The issue in my view is whether or not El Al was
justified in doing what it did.

[
79
]

The availability of this defence was conceded in
some early leading cases.

[
80
]

In
Quinn v. Leathem
,

[1901] A.C.
495
, for example, also referred to by Lord Denning in
Torquay Hotel
,
supra
,
the court held that "it is a violation of legal right to interfere with
contractual relations recognized by law if there be no
sufficient
justification
for the interference".  [Emphasis added.]

[
81
]

Despite this early acknowledgement, however, the
limits of the doctrine of justification have never been precisely defined.
Posluns
v. Toronto Stock Exchange
(1964),
1964 CanLII 199 (ON HCJ)
, 2 O.R. 547 (H.C.J.) [
Posluns
].
See also G.H.L. Fridman, The Law of Torts in Canada, 2nd. ed. (Toronto:
Carswell, 2002) at 804; L.N. Klar, Tort Law (3rd ed.) Toronto: Thompson
Carswell, 2003) at 618.

[
82
]

In the
Posluns
case, Gale J. considered
whether the defendant Toronto Stock Exchange (TSE) was justified in its
interference with the plaintiff's contract of employment as a shareholder and
director of a firm of stockbrokers which was a member of the TSE.  The TSE
sought to be excused on the ground it was justified in acting as it did since
it did so in the interest and welfare of the public.

[
83
]

Gale J. concluded that justification was rarely
a successful defence where the damage to the plaintiff was caused as a result
of an unlawful intervention.

[
84
]

He went on to find that where "the act of
interference is a
lawful
one, both as to
purpose
and
means
,
then no vindication is required unless it was committed in the course of
conspiracy to injure the victim".
Posluns
,
supra
, at 607.
[Emphasis added.]

[
85
]

As observed in
Fridman
,
supra
, at
806, Gale J. in
Posluns
seems to have felt that to support a defence of
justification, there must be some legal, that is, statutory, contractual, or
similar basis for the defendant's intervention or some significant social
reason.

[
86
]

Gale J. found there were implied contractual
obligations between the plaintiff and his employer and that the TSE interfered
pursuant to a statutory and contractual privilege.  The defence of
justification was further supported by the fact that the TSE did not resort to
illegal means to obtain the plaintiff's dismissal, but rather acted within its
by-laws and did not deny the plaintiff natural justice.
Posluns
,
supra
,
at p. 624-626.

[
87
]

In its decision in
Thermo King Corp v.
Provincial Bank of Canada
(1981),
1981 CanLII 1731 (ON CA)
, 130 D.L.R. (3d) 256 (Ont. C.A.), the
Ontario Court of Appeal indicated that for a defendant to act in his
self-interest and so to bring about a breach of contract between the plaintiff
and the third party, only amounts to justification if the defendant has a
right

to act in the way he has done.

[
88
]

In that case, the bank's assignment made it
impossible for the customer to complete a contract with the plaintiff.  The
court found that the bank was not entitled to rely on an assignment to
appropriate the funds of its customer because no money was actually due from
the customer to the bank at the material time.  As discussed in
Fridman
,

supra
, at 807, although the bank was trying to protect its interests and
finances, rather than to cause harm to the customer or to the plaintiff, it
employed "illegal means" to induce a breach of contract and thus
could not use legitimate self-interest as justification.

[
89
]

In
Edwin Hill Partners v. First NFC
,

[1988] 3 All E.R. 801
, the English Court of Appeal dealt with "equal or
superior legal right" justification, finding that justification exists
where the action taken by the defendant is to protect interference with the
defendant's own rights when they are equal or superior to the rights of the
plaintiff.  A similar conclusion was reached by the Alberta court in
Atcheson
v. College of Physicians & Surgeons (Alta.),
1994 CanLII 8933 (AB QB)
, [1994] 6 W.W.R. 239 (Alta.
Q.B.) where the defendant College had required that a doctors' clinic terminate
an arrangement it had with the plaintiff, one of the clinic’s employees.  This
led to the discharge of the plaintiff by the clinic and she sued the College
for inducing breach of contract.  The court held that the defendant College was
justified in its actions, as it was acting pursuant to its statutory
responsibility to prevent unauthorized practice of medicine.

[
90
]

The foregoing cases dealing with justification
were essentially situations where the interference complained of induced an
actual breach of contract.

[
91
]

As mentioned earlier, in
Torquay Hotel
,
supra
,
Lord Denning expanded the tort of inducing a breach of contract to those
situations where there is interference but no actual breach of the contract
ensues.

[
92
]

As pointed out in
Fridman
and in
Klar
,
this development in the tort itself has not been followed up with expansion in
the defence of justification, and that the defence is as much or more unclear
in respect of the expanded tort.

[
93
]

It seems to me this may be because the tort of
interference with business or economic relations, as discussed earlier in this
judgment requires that the defendant have committed an unlawful act, defined as
one which the defendant was not at liberty to commit.

[
94
]

However, with respect to the tort of
interference with contractual relations which do not result in a breach of that
contract, the requirement that the defendants' actions be unlawful only applies
where the defendants' interference was indirect.

[
95
]

Where the interference in the contract was
direct, regardless of whether or not it caused a breach, there is no need for
the plaintiff to prove that the defendants' actions were unlawful.

[
96
]

Since there is considerable overlap and
potentially little factual distinction between the tort of interference with
business economic relations and the tort of direct interference with
contractual relations not resulting in a breach, it is understandable there
would be some confusion in the case law since the first tort requires the
actions of the defendant be unlawful while the second one does not.

[
97
]

In the present case, for example, the actions of
El Al with respect to both YYZ and Payless can be considered in the context of
both torts.

[
98
]

It would seem strange if under the heading of
the one tort the plaintiff were required to show the defendant's acts were
unlawful, while under the other tort the plaintiff needed only show direct,
deliberate interference, without even a defence of justification available.

[
99
]

In addition, there is case law to support that
the defence of justification is available to all torts of interference of the
types in issue.

[
100
]

In
Gershman v. Manitoba Vegetable Producers’
Marketing Board
, supra,
the defendant Marketing Board resolved to blacklist
Gershman and not extend credit to any Board customer who employed him until
Gershman's debt to it was paid.  Gershman's employer let him go.

[
101
]

Although this was one of the earlier cases
considering the tort of interference with business relations, factually it
appears to be just as or even more consistent with the tort of direct
interference in an existing contractual relationship with the plaintiff losing
the opportunity to extend his existing contractual relationship of employment
into one which would include the acquisition of shares.

[
102
]

The court found on the facts that the defendant
Board did not have any reason to cause the breach of contract by the
plaintiff's employer other than the Board's history of malice, vindictiveness,
and harassment against the plaintiff in trying to collect a debt from a company
in which the plaintiff had been a shareholder.

[
103
]

The court consequently concluded that the
defendant Board acted without legal justification and for a wrongful purpose
because it was not acting in good faith or in the exercise of its official
powers.

[
104
]

In reaching its conclusions the court noted that
the plaintiff had had no control over his employer’s financial matters.  I find
that distinction to be significant since, unlike the present case, the
plaintiff was not in a position to do or potentially repeat financial harm to
the defendant.

[
105
]

The court also considered the defendant's risk
of financial loss, that is, economic justification, in the recent case of
Royal
Bank v. Wilton,
[1995] A.J. No. 247 (Alta. C.A.) (QL)
, where the defence of
justification was based on superior contractual rights.  The Alberta Court of
Appeal considered whether the bank's mortgage foreclosure proceedings caused
its client's real estate deal to fall through.  At trial, referring to
Edwin
Hill Partners v. FNFC
,
[1988] 3 All E.R. 801
, the Bank relied on the
defence of justification claiming it had a superior contractual right to that
of its client and that it was acting to protect this right.  The Court of
Appeal held that, while such defence was available, the Bank could not claim
economic justification for its interference because its interest in the
mortgage was protected and it would not have been affected by the sale of the
land by the client.  Because there was no legitimate danger that the Bank would
suffer loss as a result of the client’s actions, the Bank's foreclosure
proceedings interfered with the client’s business relations without there being
a valid justification based on a contractual right.

[
106
]

The courts have frequently seemed to mingle the
concept of unwarranted with the concept of unlawful.

[
107
]

For example, in
Posluns
,
supra
,
the court used the word "wrongful" in the context of unwarranted.

[
108
]

In
Volkswagen Canada Ltd. v. Spicer

(1978), 91 D.L.R. (3d) 42 at 61 (N.S.C.A.)
the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal held
that instructions given to the bank by the franchisor were unwarranted pursuant
to the company by-laws and therefore unlawful.

[
109
]

In the
Reach
case
, supra,
in
considering whether the conduct was unlawful, the Court of Appeal affirmed the
trial judge's finding that a letter sent by a representative of the Association
to the plaintiff's clients amounted to an improper and unwarranted act.

Conclusion

[
110
]

The initial tort of inducing a breach of
contract has been developed so that it is no longer necessary that an actual
breach is procured, nor is it necessary that there even be a contract.  As it
is consequently easier for the plaintiffs to bring forth their claims, it is
correspondingly necessary to carry through the defence of justification
particularly where there is no required element that the defendant's actions be
shown to be unlawful.

[
111
]

I have already found that El Al's actions were
not unlawful, that they were at liberty to do as they did by virtue of their
contract with the various agencies, and that El Al's concerns with respect to a
repeat performance by the plaintiff to El Al's financial detriment were
legitimate.

[
112
]

In those circumstances, I cannot see how the
acts could then be unjustified, as a consideration of whether El Al was at
liberty to commit the acts in question or whether their acts were justified
would involve a consideration of the exact same factual circumstances.

[
113
]

As pointed out by Gale J. in
Posluns
,
supra
,
at p. 607 a lawful act as to both purpose and means will seldom be unjustified
whereas an unlawful one will seldom be justified.

[
114
]

In the end, I agree with Romer L.J. in
Clamorgan
Coal v. South Wales Miner’s Fed.
, [1903] K.B. 545 (Eng. C.A.), affirmed

[1905] A.C. 239 (H.L.) where at p.573
he noted:

It would be extremely difficult, even if
it were possible, to give a complete and satisfactory definition of what is
“sufficient justification” and most attempts to do so would probably be
mischievous.

[
115
]

In my view, however, the factors to be
considered with respect to justification should at least include the following:

1.   The grounds for the interference.
For example, any statutory, contractual, or similar basis for the intervention
or some significant social reason;

2.

The purpose of the interference.  For example,
was it made in good faith or was it made in retaliation bearing in mind the
prior history of the parties.  Was there a legitimate, ie. real and reasonable,
financial interest which the defendant needed to protect;

3.

The means used.  For example, did the defendant
exceed its authority;

4.

The nature of the contract being interfered with
and the consequences of the interference.

[
116
]

El Al had a contractual right with YYZ and
Payless to terminate its
plating
agreement with them at any time for any
reason; it took steps to do so bearing in mind its prior history with the
plaintiff and its legitimate concerns in regards to its own financial
interest;  it informed each agency of the precarious position in which it found
itself as the plaintiff's involvement with each of those agencies became known
to it without attempting in any general sense to blackball or blacklist the
plaintiff in the industry;  and, finally, in the end the plaintiff's contract
with YYZ was continued but was not renewed whereas he in all likelihood still
continues his employment with Payless.  In considering the whole of the
circumstances relating to the situation of the parties, I find El Al was
justified in acting as it did.

[
117
]

For the above reasons, the plaintiff's claim
against El Al on the basis of interference, whether with business/economic
relations or with contractual relations is dismissed.

[
118
]

With respect to the remaining defendants, in his
opening statement plaintiff’s counsel stated the claim against them was
secondary as they were acting on the instructions of El Al. No closing
submissions were made concerning them. In any event, the claim against them
falls with the claim against El Al.

[
119
]

With respect to quantum of damages and an
injunction, had the plaintiff been successful in liability, I accept that the
Court may award damages at large and would have awarded such damages in the
amount of $25,000.

[
120
]

As I have already mentioned, the plaintiff was
inconsistent in whether salary or commissions were the important part of his
income, I do not have tax returns or financial statements, he appears to still
be working for Payless Travel and I am not clear on how much he is currently
making.

[
121
]

The only reasonable approach and consequence
would be to award damages at large.

[
122
]

With respect to an injunction, not only has the
plaintiff come into this without clean hands taking into account his activities
relating to the defendant surrounding the bankruptcy, but I would in any event
be reluctant to craft an injunction which might permanently require the
defendant to commit itself to business activity with those companies it would
prefer to avoid.

[
123
]

Parties may make written submissions to me with
respect to costs on or before March 3, 2006.
